title: Optimizing Joins
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of optimizing joins.
Apply reducing unnecessary joined rows in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn optimizing joins through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Optimizing Joins matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

items.title: Reducing unnecessary joined rows
items.text: Reducing unnecessary joined rows determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Join cardinality estimation
items.text: Join cardinality estimation is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Avoiding unintended Cartesian products
items.text: Avoiding unintended Cartesian products helps you explain and measure query plans, optimize based on evidence, and avoid claims that one query form is always faster. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
EXPLAIN
SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY order_date;
content_blocks.expected_output: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimated plan without executing the SELECT. Compare estimates and actual timings only with measured, representative test data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic reducing unnecessary joined rows and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
